ai.definition: Self-healing composites are advanced materials that can autonomously repair damage such as cracks and fissures to extend their service life without human intervention.
ai.howItWorks: These composites contain microcapsules or vascular networks filled with a healing agent. Upon crack formation, the capsules rupture, releasing the agent into the crack where it reacts to form a new material, effectively sealing the damage. Alternatively, reversible bonds within the composite can re-form when heated, closing the gap.
ai.problemSolved: Traditional composites and materials require maintenance or replacement after damage occurs, leading to increased costs and downtime. Self-healing composites reduce these issues by extending service life and minimizing repair needs.
ai.manufacturing: Manufacturing self-healing composites involves embedding microcapsules or vascular networks into the polymer matrix during fabrication. This can be done through various techniques such as in-situ polymerization, coating, or impregnation.
ai.buildProcess: The process typically starts with selecting a suitable base material and then incorporating healing agents or structures. The materials are then processed using standard manufacturing methods like molding, extrusion, or lamination.
ai.costDrivers: Cost drivers include the initial investment in specialized equipment for embedding microcapsules, the cost of healing agents, and potential delays in production due to complex manufacturing processes.
ai.lifecycleOutlook: The technology is expected to see increased adoption as it addresses critical needs in various industries but faces challenges related to cost and reliability.
ai.regulation: Currently, there are no specific regulations for self-healing composites, but they may fall under broader material safety guidelines. As the technology matures, regulatory frameworks will likely be developed.
ai.risks: Technical risks include ensuring consistent healing performance across different materials and environments. Economic risks involve high initial costs and potential long-term savings that may not be immediately apparent.
ai.profitability: Profitability is dependent on the specific application and market segment. While there are significant cost-saving potentials, widespread adoption requires overcoming economic barriers.
ai.futureDevelopment: Future developments will likely focus on improving healing efficiency, expanding material compatibility, and reducing production costs to make self-healing composites more accessible across a broader range of applications.

glossary.def: A property that allows materials to repair themselves autonomously without human intervention.
Tiny capsules embedded in a composite material that contain healing agents, which are released upon damage.
Networks of channels or tubes within composites that can release healing agents when damaged.

subsystems.name: Load-bearing composite
subsystems.role: provides structural integrity and is the material that cracks.

subsystems.name: Capsule-based healing system
subsystems.role: stores and releases liquid healing agent when a crack ruptures capsules.
parts: catalyst or hardener particles dispersed in matrix

subsystems.name: Vascular healing system
subsystems.role: delivers healing agent through hollow channels to repair larger or repeated damage.

subsystems.name: Reversible bond system
subsystems.role: allows the polymer itself to re-form bonds when heated or exposed to light.

subsystems.name: Trigger and control
subsystems.role: initiates healing at the right time and place.

subsystems.name: Damage sensing and verification
parts: embedded optical fibres or strain gauges

buildSteps.title: Design the composite and healing architecture
buildSteps.detail: Decide which healing mechanism to embed, where, and how it integrates with the load path, while minimising any loss of structural performance.

buildSteps.title: Produce microcapsules
buildSteps.detail: Use emulsion polymerisation to form a polymer shell around droplets of healing agent (e.g., dicyclopentadiene) in water, then dry and sieve to the target size.

buildSteps.title: Prepare catalyst or hardener
buildSteps.detail: Disperse solid catalyst (e.g., a Grubbs-type ring-opening metathesis catalyst) in the resin, or encapsulate liquid hardener in separate capsules for two-part systems.

buildSteps.title: Create vascular channels (if used)
buildSteps.detail: Weave or print sacrificial fibres (e.g., PLA) into the preform, or use 3D-printed scaffolds, then remove them after cure to leave hollow channels and reservoirs.

buildSteps.title: Mix and infuse
buildSteps.detail: Blend capsules and catalyst into resin, or infuse resin around fibres and sacrificial channels using vacuum-assisted resin transfer moulding or prepreg layup.

buildSteps.title: Cure the composite
buildSteps.detail: Apply heat and pressure to set the matrix, keeping temperatures below the point where healing agents or capsules degrade.

buildSteps.title: Test healing
buildSteps.detail: Crack samples, apply the trigger (heat, pressure, light), then measure recovery of mechanical properties such as fracture toughness or flexural strength over one or more cycles.

buildSteps.title: Scale up manufacturing
buildSteps.detail: Adapt automated fibre placement or resin transfer moulding to handle capsules and channels reliably, with quality control for capsule size, distribution and channel patency.

prerequisites.why: needed to make stable capsules that survive composite processing and release their contents only when cracked.
3D printing and sacrificial fibre techniques can create channels, but they are not yet standard in structural composite manufacturing.
dynamic bonds such as Diels–Alder work in the lab, but need higher strength, faster healing and durability over many cycles.
required to verify healing and to certify self-healing parts for safety-critical use.
must remain stable during processing, be non-toxic, and polymerise effectively within the confined crack volume.

pathway.unlocks: proof that microcapsules and vascular networks can recover a large fraction of fracture toughness, though usually only once.

pathway.milestone: pilot applications in coatings, non-structural panels and possibly wind turbine blades or aerospace secondary structures
pathway.unlocks: real-world data on durability, manufacturing compatibility and cost.

pathway.milestone: integration into primary aerospace structures or civil infrastructure with repeated healing and embedded sensing
pathway.unlocks: extended service life and reduced inspection and maintenance.

pathway.milestone: self-healing composites as standard in safety-critical structures
pathway.unlocks: lighter, more damage-tolerant designs that can recover from impacts and fatigue cracks autonomously.
